primitives.name: Optimal Play Portfolio
primitives.verbatim_quote: The innovation in our approach is to borrow from portfolio finance theory to determine the optimal share of passing and running plays.
primitives.latex: \max_{R,P} U(R,P) \text{ subject to } R + P = 1 \text{ and } U = \mathbb{E}[Y] - a \cdot \text{Var}(Y)
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'R': 'proportion of running plays, dimensionless', 'P': 'proportion of passing plays, dimensionless', 'a': 'Arrow–Pratt coefficient of absolute risk aversion, dimensionless', 'Y': 'net yardage per play, yards'}
primitives.assumptions: Coaches maximize expected net yardage adjusted for variance; play outcomes are normally distributed.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When \( a \to \infty \), risk neutrality fails and pure running becomes optimal.

primitives.name: Risk-Adjusted Utility Function
primitives.verbatim_quote: The optimal portfolio of plays maximizes a risk-averse utility function where utility is obtained from net yardage.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'U': 'utility of play mix, yards', 'Y': 'net yardage per play, yards', 'a': 'Arrow–Pratt coefficient of absolute risk aversion, dimensionless'}

primitives.verbatim_quote: By comparing the actual share of running plays to the optimal g for each NFL club, evidence can be found to support or refute Alamar's (2006) claim.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'g^*': 'optimal proportion of running plays, dimensionless', 'Y_R': 'net yardage from running plays, yards', 'Y_P': 'net yardage from passing plays, yards', '\\sigma_R^2': 'variance of running play yardage, square yards', '\\sigma_P^2': 'variance of passing play yardage, square yards', '\\text{Cov}(Y_R, Y_P)': 'covariance between running and passing yardage, square yards'}
primitives.assumptions: Expected values and variances are known; covariance reflects strategic interdependence of play types.

layer2.telemetry: Deviation \( |g - g^*| \) per team used to infer strategic misalignment.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that NFL play selection can be modeled as a portfolio optimization problem. Each play type—running or passing—is treated as an asset with expected return (net yardage) and risk (variance). The utility function incorporates both mean and variance, using Arrow–Pratt’s absolute risk aversion coefficient to weight risk. This leads to a closed-form expression for the optimal share of running plays, which depends on the difference in expected returns and variances between running and passing. Empirical validation compares this theoretical \( g^* \) with actual play shares. If teams consistently underperform in passing, it suggests a 'running premium', indicating suboptimal risk-return trade-offs. The model assumes normality of yardage distributions and static risk preferences, but allows for dynamic adjustments through \( a \). The failure mode occurs when \( a \to \infty \), implying risk neutrality, or when variances are equal, rendering the ratio undefined. These conditions highlight the limits of the model’s applicability.
